content.stem: A company whose shares have a face value of ₹40 each declares a dividend of 15%. Tanvi buys some of these shares in the market at ₹48 each. Find the percentage return on her investment.

hints: The dividend is a percentage of the face value, but the return is measured against the price Tanvi actually paid.

steps.title: Dividend per share
steps.explanation: The dividend is always calculated on the face value: ₹6 per share.
steps.rule: Dividend = rate of dividend × face value

steps.title: Rate of return
steps.explanation: Tanvi earns ₹6 for every ₹48 she invests, so her return is 12.5%.

commonMistakes: Quoting the dividend rate (15%) as the rate of return.
Calculating the dividend on the market price: \(15\% \text{ of } 48 = ₹7.20\).

criteria.description: Dividend per share on face value

questions.authorNotes: Marked by the answer key alone (numerical); the rubric is provided for the AI Examiner if working is submitted.

content.stem:
Arjun owns 600 shares of ₹100 each in Company A, which pays a dividend of 9%. He sells all these shares at ₹135 each and invests the entire proceeds in ₹20 shares of Company B available at a premium of ₹7 each. Company B pays a dividend of 12%.

Find:
(i) the number of shares of Company B that Arjun buys;
(ii) the change in his annual dividend income, stating whether it is an increase or a decrease.

hints: A premium of ₹7 on a ₹20 share means its market value is ₹27.
Compare the old income (from Company A) with the new income (from Company B), both calculated on face value.

solution.modelAnswer: Proceeds \(= 600 \times 135 = ₹81{,}000\). Market value of a B share \(= 20 + 7 = ₹27\). (i) Number of B shares \(= \tfrac{81000}{27} = 3000\). (ii) Old income \(= 600 \times 9\% \text{ of } 100 = ₹5{,}400\); new income \(= 3000 \times 12\% \text{ of } 20 = ₹7{,}200\). Change \(= 7200 - 5400 = ₹1{,}800\), an increase.

steps.title: Sale proceeds
steps.explanation: Arjun receives ₹81,000 from selling his Company A shares at the market price.

steps.title: Number of B shares
steps.explanation: Each Company B share costs its face value plus the premium, ₹27.
steps.rule: Number of shares = investment ÷ market value of one share

steps.title: Old income
steps.explanation: Dividend from Company A is 9% of the face value ₹100 = ₹9 per share.

steps.title: New income
steps.explanation: Dividend from Company B is 12% of the face value ₹20 = ₹2.40 per share.
steps.rule: Dividend = number of shares × rate × face value

commonMistakes: Using the face value ₹20 (or the premium ₹7) instead of the market value ₹27 to find the number of shares.
Calculating dividend on the market value instead of on the face value.
Using the face value ₹100 instead of the selling price ₹135 for the sale proceeds.

alternativeMethods.title: Compare returns
alternativeMethods.description: Return on the money at the time of the switch: Company A gives \(\tfrac{9}{135} \times 100 = 6\tfrac{2}{3}\%\) and Company B gives \(\tfrac{2.40}{27} \times 100 = 8\tfrac{8}{9}\%\). On ₹81,000 these give incomes of ₹5,400 and ₹7,200, so the income rises by ₹1,800.

criteria.description: Sale proceeds from Company A shares
Number of Company B shares using market value ₹27
criteria.partialCreditRules: Follow-through from an incorrect proceeds figure if ₹27 is used.

criteria.description: Both annual incomes calculated on face value
criteria.partialCreditRules: Follow-through from an incorrect number of shares.

criteria.description: Correct change stated as an increase

questions.authorNotes: Brokerage is ignored (not mentioned in the stem). The numeric answer key checks only part (ii), the change of ₹1,800; part (i) is assessed from the working.
